'''''Ulmus parvifolia''''', commonly known as the '''Chinese elm'''<ref>{{PLANTS|symbol=ULPA|taxon=Ulmus parvifolia Jacq.|access-date=7 June 2022}}</ref> or '''lacebark elm''', is a [[species]] native to eastern Asia, including China, India, Japan, Korea, Vietnam,<ref name=Fu>Fu, L., Xin, Y. & Whittemore, A. (2002). [http://flora.huh.harvard.edu/china/PDF/PDF05/Ulmus.pdf Ulmaceae], in Wu, Z. & Raven, P. (eds) ''Flora of China'', Vol. 5 (Ulmaceae through Basellaceae). Science Press, Beijing, and Missouri Botanical Garden Press, St. Louis, USA; also available as {{cite web|url=http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=2&taxon_id=200006330 |title=''Ulmus parvifolia'' |author=Fu, L. |author2=Xin, Y. |author3=Whittemore, A. |name-list-style=amp |work=Flora of China |publisher=Missouri Botanical Garden, St. Louis, Missouri & Harvard University Herbaria, Cambridge, Massachusetts |access-date=5 February 2015}}</ref> Siberia, and Kazakhstan.<ref name = "Whitcomb24">[https://drcarlwhitcomb.com/research/f/trees-of-downtown-stillwater-the-lacebark-elm Whitcomb, Dr Carl E., 'Trees of Downtown Stillwater: The Lacebark Elm' (14 August 2024); drcarlwhitcomb.com]</ref> It has been described as "one of the most splendid elms, having the poise of a graceful ''[[Nothofagus]]''".<ref name="Hilliers'">''Hilliers' Manual of Trees & Shrubs'', 4th edition, 1977, David & Charles, Newton Abbot, England</ref>

[[File:Chinese Elm April 2024.jpg|thumb|Chinese elm as [[bonsai]] during the spring growing season]]
==Description==
A small to medium [[deciduous]] or [[semideciduous]] (rarely semi[[evergreen]]) tree, it grows to {{convert|10|–|18|m|ft|abbr=on}} tall and {{convert|15|-|20|m|ft|abbr=on}} wide, with a slender trunk and crown. The leathery, lustrous green, single-toothed [[leaf|leaves]] are small, 2–5 cm long by 1–3 cm broad,<ref>{{Royal Botanic Garden Edinburgh |id=E00824803 }} ''Ulmus parvifolia'' Jacq. (1909 specimen, Breslau)</ref> and often are retained as late as December or even January in Europe and North America. In some years, the leaves take on a purplish-red autumn colour.<ref name = "Kemp">{{cite book|editor-last1=Clouston|editor-first1=Brian|editor-last2=Stansfield|editor-first2=Kathy|date=1979|title=After the Elm|page=39|chapter=The Plantsman's Elm|first=Eddie|last=Kemp|publisher=William Heinemann Ltd.|location=London|isbn=978-0-434-13900-2}}</ref> The [[apetalous]], wind-pollinated, [[perfect flower]]s are produced in early autumn, small and inconspicuous. The fruit is a [[samara (fruit)|samara]], elliptical to ovate-elliptical, 10–13 mm long by 6–8 mm broad.<ref name=Fu/> The samara is mostly [[Glabrousness|glabrous]], the seed at the centre or toward the apex, and is borne on a stalk 1–3 mm in length; it matures rapidly and disperses by late autumn. The trunk has a handsome, flaking bark of mottled greys with tans and reds, giving rise to its other common name, the lacebark elm, although scarring from major branch loss can lead to large, canker-like wounds. [[Ploidy]]: ''2n'' = 28.<ref name=Bean/><ref name=White>White, J & More, D. (2003). ''Trees of Britain & Northern Europe''. Cassell's, London.</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.cnr.vt.edu/dendro/dendrology/syllabus/uparvifolia.htm |title=Chinese elm Ulmaceae Ulmus parvifolia |website=www.cnr.vt.edu |access-date=22 May 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20001209222100/http://www.cnr.vt.edu/dendro/dendrology/syllabus/uparvifolia.htm |archive-date=9 December 2000 }}</ref><ref>{{PLANTS|symbol=ULPU|taxon=Ulmus pumila L.|access-date=7 June 2022}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.saylorplants.com/pd.asp?pid=1935 |title=SaylorPlants.com - Chinese Elm, Lacebark Elm ( Ulmus  parvifolia ) |website=www.saylorplants.com |access-date=22 May 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110716012236/http://www.saylorplants.com/pd.asp?pid=1935 |archive-date=16 July 2011 }}</ref>

Many nurserymen and foresters mistakenly refer to ''[[Ulmus pumila]]'', the rapidly growing, disease-ridden, relatively short-lived, weak-wooded Siberian elm, as "Chinese elm". This has given the true Chinese elm an undeserved bad reputation. The two elms are distinct species. The Siberian elm's bark becomes deeply ridged and furrowed with age, among other obvious differences. It possesses a very rough, greyish-black appearance, while the Chinese elm's smooth bark becomes flaky and blotchy, exposing distinctive, light-coloured mottling, hence the synonym lacebark elm for the real Chinese elm. Siberian elm produces seed in spring, Chinese elm in autumn.<ref name=Leopold>{{cite journal|last=Leopold|first=D. J.|journal=Journal of Arboriculture|title=Chinese and Siberian elms|date=1980|volume=6|issue=7|pages=175–179|url=http://joa.isa-arbor.com/request.asp?JournalID=1&ArticleID=1664&Type=2}}</ref>

==Wood and timber==
Elms, hickory, and ash all have remarkably hard, tough wood, making them popular for tool handles, bows, and baseball bats. Chinese elm is considered the hardest of the elms. It is said to be the best of all woods for chisel handles and similar uses due to its superior hardness, toughness, and resistance to splitting. Chinese elm lumber is used most for furniture, cabinets, veneer, hardwood flooring, and specialty uses such as longbow construction and tool handles. Most commercially milled lumber goes directly to manufacturers rather than to retail lumber outlets.{{citation needed|date=November 2015}}

Chinese elm heartwood ranges in tone from reddish-brown to light tan, while the sapwood approaches off-white. The grain is often handsome and dramatic. Unlike other elms, the freshly cut Chinese elm has a peppery or spicy odour. While it turns easily and will take a nice polish off the lathe without any finish, and it holds detail well, the fibrous wood is usually considered too tough for carving or hand tools. Chinese elm contains silica, which is hard on planer knives and chainsaws, but it sands fairly easily. Like other woods with interlocking grain, planes should be kept extra sharp to prevent tearing at the grain margins. It steam-bends easily and holds screws well, but pilot holes and countersinking are needed. It tends to be a "lively" wood, tending to warp and distort while drying. This water-resistant wood easily takes most finishes and stains.{{citation needed|date=September 2014}}

==Pests and diseases==
The Chinese elm is highly resistant, but not immune, to [[Dutch elm disease]]. It is also very resistant to the elm leaf beetle ''[[Xanthogaleruca luteola]]'', but has a moderate susceptibility to [[elm yellows]].<ref name=Mittempergher>{{cite journal|last1=Mittempergher|first1=L|last2=Santini|first2=A|journal=Investigacion Agraria: Sistemas y Recursos Forestales|title=The history of elm breeding|volume=13|issue=1|pages=161–177|date=2004|url=http://www.inia.es/gcontrec/Pub/161-177-(14)-The_history_1161943529015.pdf|access-date=2017-02-09|archive-date=2017-02-11|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170211155148/http://www.inia.es/gcontrec/Pub/161-177-(14)-The_history_1161943529015.pdf}}</ref> In trials at the Sunshine Nursery, Oklahoma, the species was adjudged as having the best pest resistance of about 200 taxa.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.greenbeam.com/rs/nm_pdfs/16338_013.pdf|title=greenbeam.com|website=greenbeam.com|access-date=29 March 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070928034753/http://www.greenbeam.com/rs/nm_pdfs/16338_013.pdf |archive-date=28 September 2007 |url-status=usurped}}</ref> However, foliage was regarded as only "somewhat resistant" to [[Diplocarpon rosae|black spot]] by the Plant Diagnostic Clinic of the [[University of Missouri]].<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://soilplantlab.missouri.edu/plant/diseases/resistant.htm |title=Disease resistant and tolerant plant varieties, Plant Diagnostic Clinic, MU Extension |access-date=2008-10-31 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080920051358/http://soilplantlab.missouri.edu/plant/diseases/resistant.htm |archive-date=2008-09-20 }}</ref>

[[Cottony cushion scale]] or [[mealy bugs]], often protected and "herded" by ants, exude sticky, sweet [[honeydew (secretion)|honeydew]], which can [[mildew]] leaves and be a minor annoyance by dripping on cars and furniture. However, severe infestations on or obvious damage to otherwise healthy trees are uncommon.{{citation needed|date=April 2018}}

In some regions of the Southern United States, a fungus known as [[Texas root rot]] (''Phymatotrichopsis omnivora'') is known to cause sudden death of lacebark elms when infected.{{citation needed|date=March 2023}} [[Alan Mitchell (botanist)|Alan Mitchell]] reported (1984) that established trees at [[Kew Gardens]] and at Royal Victoria Park, [[Bath, Somerset|Bath]], had been killed by [[Armillaria mellea|honey fungus]].<ref>Mitchell, Alan, & Jobling, John, ''Decorative Trees for Country, Town, and Garden'' (London, 1984), p.99</ref>

==Cultivation==
The Chinese elm is a tough landscape tree, hardy enough for use in harsh planting situations such as parking lots, small planters along streets, and plazas or patios. The tree is arguably the most ubiquitous elm, now found on all continents except Antarctica. It was introduced to Europe at the end of the 18th century as an ornamental, and is found in many botanical gardens and arboreta.<ref>{{cite web|website=Herbarium catalogue|title=Ulmus parvifolia Jacq. (1854) K000852632|publisher=Board of Trustees of the Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew|access-date=17 October 2016|url=http://apps.kew.org/herbcat/getImage.do?imageBarcode=K000852632}}; {{cite web|website=Herbarium catalogue|title=Ulmus parvifolia Jacq. (1867) K000852633|publisher=Board of Trustees of the Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew|access-date=17 October 2016|url=http://apps.kew.org/herbcat/getImage.do?imageBarcode=K000852633}}; {{cite web|website=Herbarium catalogue|title=Ulmus sieboldii Daveau (1913) K000852631|publisher=Board of Trustees of the Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew|access-date=17 October 2016|url=http://apps.kew.org/herbcat/getImage.do?imageBarcode=K000852631}}</ref><ref name=Ryston>{{cite book| title=Ryston Hall Arboretum catalogue |date=c. 1920 |pages=13–14|url=https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Ryston_Hall_Arboretum_Catalogue_c._1920_pages_13,14.jpg}}</ref> The tree was introduced to the UK in 1794 by [[James Main (botanist)|James Main]], who collected in China for Gilbert Slater of [[Low Layton]], Essex.<ref name=Elwes>Elwes, H. J. & Henry, A. (1913). ''[http://fax.libs.uga.edu/QK488xE4/1f/trees_of_britain_and_ireland_vol_7.pdf The Trees of Great Britain & Ireland] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160303174627/http://fax.libs.uga.edu/QK488xE4/1f/trees_of_britain_and_ireland_vol_7.pdf |date=2016-03-03 }}''. Vol. VII. 1848–1929. Republished 2004 Cambridge University Press, {{ISBN|9781108069380}}</ref><ref name=Bean>Bean, W. J. (1981). ''Trees and shrubs hardy in Great Britain'', 7th edition. Murray, London.</ref> It was also introduced to the United States in 1794,<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://archive.org/details/mobot31753002462148|title=Missouri Botanical Garden bulletin.|date=29 March 1913|publisher=[St. Louis : Missouri Botanical Garden]|access-date=29 March 2022|website=Archive.org}}</ref> where, before the introduction of cold-hardy forms from the 1990s, it was mainly planted in southern States and in California.<ref name = "Karnosky88"/> It has proved very popular in recent years as a replacement for [[American elm]]s killed by Dutch elm disease. The tree was distributed in [[Victoria (Australia)|Victoria]], Australia, from 1857.<ref name = "Brookes&Barley 1992">{{Cite web|url=https://trove.nla.gov.au/work/34926332?selectedversion=NBD9147128|title=Trove|website=Trove.nla.gov.au|access-date=29 March 2022}}</ref> At the beginning of the 20th century, Searl's Garden Emporium, in Sydney, marketed it.{{Citation needed|date=October 2017}} Three ''U. parvifolia''  were supplied in 1902 by [[Späth nursery|Späth]] to the [[Royal Botanic Garden Edinburgh]].<ref name=Edinburgh>{{cite book |date=1902|title=Accessions book|publisher=Royal Botanic Garden Edinburgh|pages=45, 47|url=https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Royal_Botanic_Garden_Edinburgh._(1902)._Accessions_book_pages_45,47.jpg}}</ref><ref>{{Royal Botanic Garden Edinburgh |id=E00824804 }} ''Ulmus parvifolia'' Jacq. (1902, [[Späth nursery]]); {{Royal Botanic Garden Edinburgh |id=E00824805 }} ''Ulmus parvifolia'' Jacq. (1902, Späth); {{Royal Botanic Garden Edinburgh |id=E00824802 }} ''Ulmus parvifolia'' Jacq. (1902, Späth)</ref> In New Zealand, it was found to be particularly suitable for windswept locations along the coast. The tree is commonly planted as an ornamental in Japan,<ref name=Hishiyama>Hishiyama, C. (Ed.). (2018). ''A picture book of (Japanese) trees'',  p.81. (in Japanese). Seibidoshuppan, Japan. {{ISBN|9784415310183}}</ref> notably around [[Osaka Castle]].

''U. parvifolia'' is one of the cold-hardiest of the Chinese species. In artificial freezing tests at the [[Morton Arboretum]].<ref name=Shirazi>Shirazi, A. M. & Ware, G. H. (2004). ===Bonsai===
Owing to its versatility and ability to tolerate a wide range of temperatures, light, and humidity conditions, the Chinese elm is a popular choice as a [[bonsai]] species. It is perhaps the single most widely available. It is considered a good choice for beginners because of its high tolerance of pruning.<ref name="Ma-Ke_Ulmus parvifolia ">{{cite web | first=Mark | last=D'Cruz | title=Ma-Ke Bonsai Care Guide for Ulmus parvifolia | date=11 February 2020 | publisher=Ma-Ke Bonsai | url=https://www.makebonsai.com/post/chinese-elm | access-date=2021-02-04}}</ref>

==Naturalisation==
[[File:UlmusParv1.jpg|thumb|right|200px|Naturalised ''U. parvifolia'' establishing itself by a roadside, Greensboro, North Carolina (2022)]]
''U. parvifolia'' has become naturalised in various parts of the US, including Idaho, Oklahoma, West Virginia, and Kentucky.<ref>[http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=1&taxon_id=200006330 ''U. parvifolia'', Flora of North America, efloras.org]</ref><ref>[https://www.jstor.org/stable/41961085 Max E. Medley and John W. Thieret, 'U. parvifolia naturalized in Kentucky'; SIDA, Contributions to Botany, Vol. 14, No. 4, December 1991, pp. 610-613 (4 pages), The Botanical Research Institute of Texas]</ref><ref>[https://ag.ok.gov/trees-of-oklahoma/ Urban and Community Trees of Oklahoma, ag.ok.gov]</ref>  It is listed as invasive in District of Columbia, North Carolina, Nebraska, New Jersey, Virginia, and Wisconsin.<ref>USDA Forest Service, Forest Health Staff, Invasive Plants website: na.fs.fed.us/fhp/invasive_plants/weeds/chinese-elm.pdf</ref><ref>[https://www.cirrusimage.com/tree_chinese_elm/ ''U. parvifolia'', cirrusimage.com]</ref> As a "garden escape" it has also become naturalised in South Africa, where in 1904 it was described as "common near [[Irene, Gauteng|Irene]]",<ref>[http://n2t.net/ark:/65665/m30fb32691-4ea0-4adc-ab58-4d5cdda35478 ''U. parvifolia'' specimen, Transvaal Department of Agriculture, in collections.nmnh.si.edu, herbarium specimen 03413443]</ref> and in 1980 as "occasional" in [[Moreleta Park]], both near Pretoria.<ref>[http://n2t.net/ark:/65665/m3795a830e-eb0c-470b-ad3e-ee389a4b33a3 ''U. parvifolia'' specimen, National Herbarium Pretoria, in collections.nmnh.si.edu, herbarium specimen 03413521]</ref>   

==Notable trees==
The tree in [[Central Park]], New York City, planted in 1865 by James Hogg,<ref>''Garden and Forest'', i. 231, 312 (1888)</ref><ref name=Elwes/> from which the cultivar {{tdes|Central Park Splendor|caps}} was cloned, was believed to be the oldest specimen of lacebark elm in the US at the time of its death in the 1990s, with a diameter at breast height of 1.4 m.<ref name = "Karnosky88">'Aross (sic) Central Park' Chinese Elm, by David F. Karnosky, HortScience 23(5):925-926, 1988</ref>

==Etymology==
The name "lacebark elm", referring to the distinctive patchwork bark patterns, was suggested by E. W. Johnson of the Woodward, Oklahoma, USDA research station (who received ''U. parvifolia'' seed sent from the Far East by collector [[Frank Nicholas Meyer|Frank Meyer]] around 1908), to reduce confusion with the Siberian elm, ''U. pumila'', also called Chinese elm in the early days. Carl E. Whitcomb of [[Oklahoma State University]], who raised the cultivar 'Prairie Shade', reintroduced the name "lacebark elm" in his ''Know It and Grow It: A Guide to the Identification and Use of Landscape Plants'' (1975).<ref name = "Whitcomb24"/>
